x.t: Helpers kept people safe as Cyclone Akvan grew weaker
b: Because of [[cyclone|Cyclone]] Akvan, helpers in Odisha moved over 4.4 lakh people to safety. A lakh is one hundred thousand.
The storm came onto land near [[gopalpur|Gopalpur]] on Friday 20 November. By Friday evening it had become weaker. Officials said no big damage had been reported.
Lighter rain was expected from Saturday. More than 400 teams were ready to help. Some teams were sent to clear away rainwater.

o.t: Helpers moved over 4.4 lakh people to safety as Akvan weakened
b: More than 4.4 lakh (440,000) people in Odisha were moved to safety because of [[cyclone|Cyclone]] Akvan, officials said. Thousands of cyclone [[shelter|shelters]] had been made ready. More than 400 teams were in place to help, including rescue teams and fire service teams.

Akvan crossed the coast near [[gopalpur|Gopalpur]] on the morning of Friday 20 November. It then weakened step by step. By Friday evening it was a depression, a much weaker kind of weather system than a cyclone. Weather experts expected it to weaken further as it moved north over Odisha.

Officials said no major damage had been reported. Teams worked to clear roads and were sent to clear away rainwater. The rain was expected to ease from Saturday, but heavy rain was still forecast for Mayurbhanj and Balasore districts.

stories.think: Many people moved to safe places because of the storm. How does your family get ready when a big storm or heavy rain is coming?

quiz.q: Near which place did Cyclone Akvan cross the coast?

x.t: Climate talks go into extra time
b: Climate talks in Turkey should have ended on Friday 20 November. They ran late.
Nearly 200 countries took part. By Friday evening they had not agreed on a deal. They disagreed about [[fossil-fuels|fossil fuels]]: coal, oil and gas. These heat the planet.
Some wanted the deal to mention them. Countries that produce oil objected. Poorer countries wanted more money from richer ones. A new [[draft|draft]], or early version, was expected.

o.t: COP31 climate talks miss their deadline and go into overtime
b: [[cop31|COP31]], the United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, was scheduled to end on Friday 20 November. It ran into overtime, or extra time. By Friday evening, the nearly 200 countries taking part had still not reached a deal.
A deal at the talks needs [[consensus|consensus]], or general agreement, among the countries. But on Friday the countries were divided over what the deal should say.

A [[draft|draft]], or early version, of the deal was shared on Thursday. It left out [[fossil-fuels|fossil fuels]], the coal, oil and gas that heat the planet. Several countries objected and said the deal must mention fossil fuels. Oil-producing countries had resisted such wording. Poorer countries wanted more money from richer ones to cope with climate change. A new draft was expected.

stories.think: Think of a time when your family or friends could not agree on something. What helped you to find an answer that everyone could accept?

quiz.q: Why did the climate talks run past their finishing day?

Because only one country is allowed to speak
Because the countries had not agreed on a deal
Because the deal has to be very short

x.t: A cheetah from Botswana has four cubs in India
b: A mother cheetah has had four [[cubs|cubs]]. They were born on Friday 20 November at [[kuno|Kuno National Park]] in India.
The cubs were born [[in-the-wild|in the wild]]. That means free in nature. Their mother had lived in the wild for more than four months.
She was brought to India from [[botswana|Botswana]]. India has a plan to bring cheetahs back. With the new cubs, India now has 62 cheetahs.

o.t: Cheetah from Botswana has four cubs in the wild at Kuno
b: A female cheetah known as KOMG 3 gave birth to four [[cubs|cubs]] [[in-the-wild|in the wild]] on Friday 20 November. In the wild means living freely in nature. The cubs were born at [[kuno|Kuno National Park]] in Madhya Pradesh. KOMG 3 had spent more than four months in the wild before her cubs arrived.

KOMG 3 is about two and a half years old. India has a programme to bring cheetahs back to the country. KOMG 3 was brought to India from [[botswana|Botswana]]. She is the first female cheetah from Botswana to give birth in India.
The news was shared on the social media site X by [[bhupender-yadav|Bhupender Yadav]], India's environment minister. With the four new cubs, the number of cheetahs in India has gone up to 62.

stories.think: The mother cheetah lived in the wild for months before her cubs were born. What do you think a wild animal needs to bring up its young?

x.t: Potatoes grow well in fake Moon soil with worm compost
b: Could food grow on the Moon one day? Scientists tested this with potatoes in [[simulated|fake]] Moon soil.
Moon dust has very little in it from living things. So they mixed in [[compost|compost]] made by worms. Compost helps plants grow.
The mix was 30 parts compost in every 100. With it, potatoes grew about as well as in Earth soil. Next comes a study of 10 kinds of potato.

o.t: Worm compost helps potatoes grow in simulated Moon soil
b: Scientists at Oregon State University have grown potatoes in [[simulated|simulated]] Moon soil. Simulated means not real, but made to be like the real thing. The study, in the journal npj Microgravity, was reported on Thursday 19 November.

[[regolith|Regolith]] is the layer of rock and dust on the Moon's surface. It holds very little organic matter, meaning material from living things. So the team mixed [[compost|compost]] made by worms into their simulated soil. Without the compost, the plants did not grow properly. With 30 per cent compost, or 30 parts in every 100, they grew about as well as in Earth soil.

The scientists believe the compost also helps protect plants from harmful metals in the regolith. They say this is a step towards growing food for people exploring the Moon. Next comes a study of 10 varieties, or types, of potato.

stories.think: If you lived on the Moon, which food would you most want to grow there, and why?

quiz.q: What did the scientists mix into the fake Moon soil to help the potatoes grow?

x.t: Lakshya Sen and an Indian pair reach badminton semi-finals
b: India's Lakshya Sen won again in Hong Kong on Friday. That made 13 [[badminton|badminton]] wins in a row.
He lost the second game but still won. A match is the best of three games. Lakshya won two of them.
Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty won in [[doubles|doubles]], with two players on each side. They and Lakshya reached the [[semi-final|semi-finals]], the round before the final.

o.t: Lakshya Sen and doubles pair reach Hong Kong Open semi-finals
b: India's Lakshya Sen has reached the [[semi-final|semi-finals]], the round before the final, at the Hong Kong Open, a [[badminton|badminton]] tournament. On Friday 20 November he won his [[quarter-final|quarter-final]], the round before the semi-finals, against a former world champion. It was his 13th win in a row.

The score was 21-17, 10-21, 21-13. That is three games, and he lost the second. But a match is the best of three games, and he won the first and the third. In [[doubles|doubles]], with two players on each side, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty also lost their second game, then won to reach the semi-finals.
Rakshitha Ramraj, 19, lost her quarter-final in two games. Earlier in the tournament she had beaten an Olympic champion from China.

stories.think: By Friday, Lakshya Sen had won 13 matches in a row. What do you think helps a player to keep winning, match after match?

x.t: Google plans to try AI computers in space
b: Google said on Thursday that it had booked a rocket to try computers in space.

The rocket is meant to launch [[satellite|satellites]], machines that travel around Earth, early in 2029. They would hold computer parts for [[ai|AI]], which lets computers copy intelligent human behaviour.
AI needs lots of electricity. On the satellites' path, sunlight could power them almost all the time. It is only a plan, and testing continues.

o.t: Google plans a 2029 rocket launch for sun-powered AI satellites
b: Google and rocket company Blue Origin announced an agreement on Thursday 19 November. Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket is to launch [[satellite|satellites]], machines travelling around Earth, for Project Suncatcher. That is Google's research into computing in space for [[ai|AI]], or artificial intelligence. The launch is targeted for the first three months of 2029.

AI means computer systems that can copy intelligent human behaviour, and it uses lots of electricity. The satellites are to carry Google's AI [[chip|chips]], very small parts holding electronic circuits. Their planned [[orbit|orbit]], or path around Earth, gets sunlight almost all the time. Google says [[solar-panel|solar panels]], which turn sunlight into electricity, can produce up to eight times more power there than on Earth.
Testing continues: chips in space cannot be cooled by air, so they need another way to lose heat. Google plans to link two satellites in 2027.

stories.think: What is one good thing and one tricky thing about putting computers in space?

x.t: Britain and the European Union agree three new deals
b: Britain was once part of the [[european-union|European Union]], a group of European countries. It left, and that is called [[brexit|Brexit]].
On Friday 20 November, leaders from both sides met in Brussels. They agreed three deals. One is for young adults. They could live, work or study on the other side for up to three years.
The leaders welcomed the deals. Some politicians in Britain do not like them.

o.t: Britain and EU agree three deals, including a youth scheme
b: Britain used to belong to the [[european-union|European Union]], or EU, a group of European countries. Its exit is known as [[brexit|Brexit]]. On Friday 20 November, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders agreed three deals at a [[summit|summit]], or leaders' meeting, in Brussels.

One will cut paperwork and checks on food sold abroad. Another will link their carbon markets, where companies buy and sell permits to release polluting gases. The third will let up to 100,000 young adults from each side live, work or study on the other side for up to three years.

People disagree about the deals. Mr Burnham called it a good day for Britain and Europe. Opposition politicians criticised the deals, and the party Reform UK called them a betrayal, or breaking of trust. University fees for EU students are still to be negotiated.

stories.think: If you could spend a year living in another country when you are grown up, where would you go, and what would you like to learn there?

Become leaders of the European Union
Stay on the other side for ever

x.t: A new insect that swims upside down is found in India
b: Scientists in India have found a new kind of insect. It is a [[backswimmer|backswimmer]], so it swims upside down.
It was found in fresh water in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
To check it was new, scientists studied its body and [[dna|DNA]]. DNA holds the instructions inside living things. Small pools and streams may hold more living things nobody has recorded.

o.t: New upside-down swimming insect found in two Indian reserves
b: Scientists from the Zoological Survey of India have discovered a new [[species|species]], or kind, of insect. It is a [[backswimmer|backswimmer]], an insect that swims upside down beneath the water surface. The find was reported this week.
The insect was found in fresh water in two reserves. They are the Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve in Andhra Pradesh and the Amrabad Tiger Reserve in Telangana.

To check it was new, the team studied its body and its [[dna|DNA]], the chemical that carries instructions inside living things. The DNA tests showed a difference of about 10 to 14.5 per cent, or parts in every 100, from related species. That supports calling it a separate species. A survey scientist said small rock pools and forest streams may hold species not yet recorded.

stories.think: What small living things have you noticed in or near water, and what would you like to find out about them?

x.t: Eight European football teams find out who they will play
b: A football [[draw|draw]] was held in [[nyon|Nyon]] on Friday. A draw picks by chance who plays whom. It put the teams of eight European countries into four pairs.
Spain will play France. Norway will play England. The Netherlands will play Portugal. Belgium will play Germany.
Each pair will play two games in March 2027, one in each country. The winners reach the [[semi-final|semi-finals]], the round before the final.

o.t: Spain to face France in Nations League quarter-finals
b: The draw for the quarter-finals of the [[nations-league|UEFA Nations League]] was held in [[nyon|Nyon]], Switzerland, on Friday 20 November. The Nations League is a football competition for the national teams of Europe. A [[draw|draw]] decides by chance which teams play each other. This one put the eight teams in the quarter-finals, the round before the semi-finals, into four pairs. These contests are called ties.

The ties are Spain v France, Norway v England, the Netherlands v Portugal, and Belgium v Germany. Each tie will be two matches, a first leg and a return leg, in late March 2027, with one match in each team's country.
The draw also set the path to the [[semi-final|semi-finals]], the round before the final. The winner of Belgium v Germany will meet the winner of Norway v England.

stories.think: If you were in charge of a football competition, would you pick who plays whom with a draw, or in another way? Why?

quiz.q: Which team will England play in March 2027?

x.t: Films from 86 countries are showing in Goa
b: A film [[festival|festival]] opened in Goa on Friday. It lasts nine days. An [[orchestra|orchestra]], a group of musicians, played at the opening.
At a film festival, many films are shown. This one has films from 86 countries. So people can watch stories from far away.
The orchestra was led by Ricky Kej, who writes music. The festival's main idea is "Stories Without Borders".

o.t: India's international film festival opens in Goa for nine days
b: The 57th International Film Festival of India opened in Goa on Friday 20 November. A film [[festival|festival]] is an event where many films are shown. This festival runs for nine days and has more than 150 films from 86 countries, so audiences in Goa can watch stories from other parts of the world.

At the opening, an [[orchestra|orchestra]], a group of musicians, performed. It was led by the composer Ricky Kej. A composer is a person who writes music. The festival's theme, or main idea, is "Stories Without Borders".

The opening ceremony was held at the Dr Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Stadium. Actors Kartik Aaryan and Sai Pallavi were there. The festival's director, Ashutosh Gowariker, spoke at the ceremony. Goa's Chief Minister, Pramod Sawant, shared an idea for the future: a film city with facilities for making films.

stories.think: Think of a film or story you like that comes from another place. What did it show you about how people live there?

x.t: Not every child gets a year of learning before primary school
b: Friday 20 November was World Children's Day. A new world report about young children came out that day.
It is about learning before [[primary-school|primary school]], called [[pre-primary|pre-primary education]]. The report says about 6 in 10 children get at least one year.
The report says more people are needed to teach young children. It says more money is needed too, so every child gets that year.

o.t: About 6 in 10 children get a year of early learning, report says
b: On Friday 20 November, World Children's Day, a report about young children's learning was launched in Paris. It was published by [[unesco|UNESCO]], the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, with partner organisations.

It looks at [[pre-primary|pre-primary education]], which means organised learning before [[primary-school|primary school]], for example at a preschool. The report says about 59 per cent of children starting primary school have had at least one year of it. That is 59 in every 100, or about 6 in 10. The report says this share has barely changed since 2015.

The report says about 6 million more pre-primary educators, people whose job is to teach, are needed by 2030. It says more money is needed each year to give every child at least one year. UNESCO is helping countries including Jamaica, Morocco and Tanzania with their planning.

stories.think: What do you think young children should get to learn and do before they start class 1?

quiz.q: According to the report, about how many children get at least one year of learning before primary school?

x.t: New world records for parking, painting and skipping
b: People in many places set [[world-record|world records]] for Guinness World Records Day. It was on Thursday. A stunt driver parked a car in a tight space, balanced on two wheels.
A painter made a painting of the Statue of Liberty in 43.5 seconds. In Dubai, 12 cars did [[donut|donuts]], fast tight turns, in one circle.
One person did 249 rope skips in one minute, wearing flip-flops!

o.t: Two-wheel parking and speed painting among new world records
b: People around the world set new [[world-record|world records]] for Guinness World Records Day 2026, which was on Thursday 19 November. A world record is the best result ever recorded anywhere in the world. Stunt driver Alastair Moffatt set a record for parking a car in the tightest space while driving it balanced on two wheels.

Performance painter David Garibaldi set a record by painting a picture of the Statue of Liberty in 43.5 seconds. In Dubai, the 777 Drifting Team had 12 cars doing [[donut|donuts]], which are fast, tight turns, at the same time in a single circle.
In Japan, one person set three [[rope-skipping|rope-skipping]] records, and a person in Indonesia did 249 rope skips in one minute while wearing flip-flops.

stories.think: If you could try to set a safe record, like skipping or stacking, what would you choose, and how would you practise?

cyclone: A powerful storm with strong winds that spin around. It often brings heavy rain.
A powerful storm in which strong winds move in a circle, often bringing heavy rain. Weather experts describe cyclones by strength: a severe cyclonic storm is stronger than a cyclonic storm.
gopalpur: A place on the coast of Odisha.
A place on the coast of Odisha. Cyclone Akvan crossed the coast near it on Friday 20 November.
shelter: A place that protects people from bad weather or danger.
A place or building that protects people from bad weather or danger. A cyclone shelter is a building that protects people during a cyclone.
consensus: When the members of a group all agree.
Agreement among the members of a group. A deal at the United Nations climate talks needs consensus among the countries.
cop31: A big meeting where countries talk about the climate.
The United Nations climate conference held in Antalya, Turkey, where countries talk about the climate.
draft: An early version of a piece of writing, not the final one.
An early version of a piece of writing, such as an agreement, made before the final version.
fossil-fuels: Coal, oil and gas. People burn them as fuel.
Fuels such as coal, oil and gas, formed underground over a very long time. People burn them.
bhupender-yadav: India's Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
botswana: The country the mother cheetah was brought from.
A country. KOMG 3, the mother of the new cubs, was brought to India from there.
cubs: Young meat-eating animals, such as young lions, bears or foxes.
The young of some meat-eating animals, such as lions, bears and foxes.
in-the-wild: Living free in nature, not controlled by people.
Living in a natural place that is not controlled by people.
kuno: A national park in Madhya Pradesh, a state of India.
A national park in the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh. KOMG 3, a cheetah brought from Botswana, lives there.
compost: Rotted plants, mixed into soil to help plants grow.
A mixture of decayed plants that is added to soil to help plants grow. The compost in this study was made by worms.
regolith: The layer of rock and dust on the surface of the Moon.
The layer of rock and dust that covers the Moon's surface.
simulated: Made to be like something real, but not the real thing.
Not real, but made to look, feel or behave like the real thing.
badminton: A game where players hit a shuttlecock over a net with rackets.
A racket game in which players hit a shuttlecock back and forth over a net.
doubles: A game with two players on each side.
A game, in sports such as badminton and tennis, in which one pair of players plays against another pair.
quarter-final: One of four matches that decide who reaches the semi-finals.
One of the four matches that decide which players or teams go on to the semi-finals.
semi-final: One of two matches that decide who plays in the final.
One of the two matches that decide who plays in the final.
ai: Short for artificial intelligence. It lets computers copy intelligent human behaviour.
Short for artificial intelligence: computer systems that can copy intelligent human behaviour.
chip: A very small part inside a computer that holds electronic circuits.
A very small piece of material that holds electronic circuits, used inside computers.
orbit: The path something follows as it travels around a planet.
The curved path that an object in space follows as it moves around a planet, star or moon.
satellite: A machine sent into space that travels around Earth.
A machine that is sent into space and moves around Earth or another planet.
solar-panel: A panel that turns sunlight into electricity.
A piece of equipment that uses light from the Sun to produce electricity.
brexit: The United Kingdom leaving the European Union.
The United Kingdom's exit from the European Union.
european-union: A group that many European countries belong to.
An economic and political organisation that many European countries belong to. It is often called the EU.
summit: A meeting between the leaders of two or more governments.
backswimmer: A water insect that swims upside down.
A water insect that swims upside down beneath the water surface.
dna: The instructions inside living things for how they grow and work.
The chemical in the cells of living things that carries the instructions for how they grow and work.
species: One kind of animal or plant.
A group of animals or plants that are alike and can have young together.
draw: A way of choosing by chance who will play whom.
A way of deciding by chance which teams will play each other in a competition.
nations-league: A football contest for the national teams of Europe.
The UEFA Nations League, a competition for the national teams of Europe.
nyon: A place in Switzerland. The draw was held there.
A place in Switzerland, where the draw for the quarter-finals was held.
festival: A special time when people celebrate, or an event with lots of films, music or plays.
A day or time of celebration. It can also be an organised series of performances, such as films, music or plays.
orchestra: A group of musicians who play music together.
A group of musicians who play together, led by a conductor.
pre-primary: Learning for young children before they start primary school, for example at a preschool.
Organised learning for young children before they start primary school, for example at a preschool. The report counts children who have had at least one year of it.

unesco: A United Nations organisation that works on education, science and culture.
The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. Its headquarters are in Paris.
donut: A fast, tight turn in which a car goes round in a full circle.
A fast, tight turn in which a car is driven round in a full circle (360 degrees).
rope-skipping: Jumping over a rope as it swings under your feet.
Jumping over a rope each time it is swung over your head and under your feet.
world-record: The best result that anyone in the world has ever reached.
The best result ever recorded anywhere in the world.
light-day: How far light travels in one whole day. It is a very long way.
A unit of distance: how far light travels in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion kilometres.
interstellar: The space between the stars. Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to enter it, in 2012.
jpl: A NASA centre in California. The Voyager 1 mission is run from there.
A NASA laboratory in California. The Voyager mission is run from there.
deep-space-network: NASA's big antennas that keep track of faraway spacecraft.
NASA's network of giant radio antennas, with sites in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. It keeps track of Voyager 1.

Rescue worker (a person trained to help and move people to safety in emergencies)
Firefighter (a person trained to put out fires and help people in emergencies such as floods)

g-cop31.ctx: No COP climate summit has finished on time since 2003. In recent years the summits have often run more than 24 hours past their planned end. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed to transition, or move, away from fossil fuels.
g-cop31.ask: Climate summits have a set finishing day, but they have not ended on time for many years. Some people think a deadline is still useful, because it pushes negotiators to make hard choices instead of talking for ever. Others think a deadline makes people rush, and that talks this important should take as long as they need. Does a deadline help people to reach a good agreement, or does it get in the way?
jobs: Diplomat (a person who represents their country in talks with other countries)
Interpreter (a person who puts what someone says into another language as they speak)
Environmental lawyer (a lawyer who works on laws and agreements that protect nature and the climate)

in-cheetah-cubs.ctx: The programme to bring cheetahs back began in 2022. Since then, 43 of India's 62 cheetahs have been born in India, and KOMG 3's cubs are only the second recorded birth in the wild.
in-cheetah-cubs.ask: Some people think animals brought to a new country should be released into the wild as soon as they can, so they live freely and raise young on their own. Others think they should stay longer in places where people can look after them closely. Which do you think is better for the animals, and why?
jobs: Wildlife vet (an animal doctor who cares for wild animals)
Forest ranger (a person who looks after a forest or park and the animals that live there)
Wildlife biologist (a scientist who studies wild animals and how they live)

g-moon-potatoes.ctx: Regolith was made over billions of years, as rocks from space hit the Moon. Potatoes give more calories, a measure of the energy in food, for each area of land than many other crops. Tests found no significant rise in the natural toxins, or poisonous substances, found in potatoes, though some potatoes held more copper, zinc or aluminium.
g-moon-potatoes.ask: The researchers say this work is a step towards growing food for people exploring the Moon. Some people think it is worth spending time and money now to learn how to farm in space. Others think that effort should go first to helping people grow food in poor soil on Earth. Which view do you find stronger, or could the same research help both?
jobs: Plant scientist (a scientist who studies how plants grow and what they need)
Soil scientist (a scientist who studies soil and how to keep it healthy)
Astronaut (a person trained to travel and work in space)

in-badminton-semis.ctx: Lakshya Sen recently won two tournaments, the Hylo Open and the Kumamoto Masters Japan. Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty came to Hong Kong after going out in the first round of their previous three tournaments.
in-badminton-semis.ask: A badminton match is the best of three games, so a player can lose one game and still win. Some contests, such as a running race, are decided in a single go. Is a best-of-three match a fairer way to find the better player, or is a single game more exciting because every point counts more?
jobs: Badminton coach (a person who trains players and helps them plan how to play)
Sports physiotherapist (a person who helps athletes stay fit and recover from injuries)
Sports journalist (a person who reports on matches and players)

g-suncatcher.ctx: A prototype for the project, meaning a first model of something new, was made with the company Planet and launched in October on a SpaceX flight. In space it ran an AI model called Gemma 4, which sent back a haiku, a poem of three lines. The 2029 flight is planned as a launch dedicated to Project Suncatcher, which means it is used for that one purpose only.
g-suncatcher.ask: Some people think putting AI computers in space is a clever way to use the Sun's power without taking more electricity on Earth. Others think the effort would be better spent on making computers on the ground use less electricity. Which idea do you find more convincing, and could both be worth trying?
jobs: Aerospace engineer (a person who designs rockets and spacecraft)
Chip designer (a person who plans the tiny circuits inside computer chips)
Thermal engineer (an engineer who works out how to stop machines getting too hot)

g-uk-eu-deal.ctx: Efforts to bring Britain and the EU closer again began under the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer. Friday's meeting was the second yearly summit between the two sides. Under the food deal, Britain will follow some EU food rules.
g-uk-eu-deal.ask: Under the food deal, there will be fewer checks on food that Britain sells to the EU, and Britain will follow some EU food rules. Some people think sharing a neighbour's rules is a fair price for easier trade. Others think a country should make all of its own rules, even if that makes trade harder. When is it worth sharing rules with your neighbours, and when is it better to make your own?
jobs: Trade negotiator (a person who works out trade deals between countries)
Customs officer (a person who checks goods as they cross a border)
Political reporter (a journalist who explains what governments and political parties are doing)

in-backswimmer.ctx: The team, from the Zoological Survey of India in Hyderabad and VHNSN College in Virudhunagar, named the insect Enithares deccanensis and published its study in the Journal of Natural History. The new backswimmer has a dark V-shaped mark on its wings and occurs in light and dark colour forms. The survey's director, Dhriti Banerjee, said the find shows the importance of surveying biodiversity, the variety of living things, and of protecting freshwater habitats in the Eastern Ghats, where the insect was found.
in-backswimmer.ask: Surveys that look for small, little-known animals take time and money. Some people think that effort is better spent protecting animals we already know are in danger. Others think a place cannot be protected well until we know what lives there. Which argument do you find stronger, and why?
jobs: Entomologist (a scientist who studies insects)
Taxonomist (a scientist who describes, names and groups living things)
Freshwater ecologist (a scientist who studies life in rivers, lakes, streams and pools)

g-nations-league.ctx: In each tie, the team named second plays the return leg at home. Germany, for example, play the first leg in Belgium and the return leg in Germany, both in late March 2027. The four winners go on to single-match semi-finals on 9 and 10 June 2027, with the final on 13 June, and Portugal are the current holders of the title.
g-nations-league.ask: In each tie, one team plays the second match at home. Some people think that is an advantage, because that team has its home crowd for the deciding match. Others think it makes no real difference, because each team gets one match at home. Does it matter which team plays at home last?
jobs: Football coach (a person who trains a team and plans how it plays)
Football referee (an official who makes sure players follow the rules during a match)
Sports event organiser (a person who plans where and when matches are played)

in-iffi-opens.ctx: The festival's opening film is "Fatherland", directed by Pawel Pawlikowski. Alongside the festival runs the WAVES Film Bazaar, which brings film-makers together with distributors.
in-iffi-opens.ask: The festival's theme is "Stories Without Borders". Some people say watching films from other countries is one of the best ways to understand how people live there. Others say a film shows only one film-maker's view, so it can give a narrow picture of a place. How much can a film really teach you about another country?
jobs: Composer (a person who writes music, for example for films)
Film editor (a person who chooses and joins filmed shots to make the finished film)
Subtitler (a person who writes the translated words shown on screen, so people can follow a film in another language)

g-early-learning.ctx: A goal for 2030 is that all girls and boys have access to quality early childhood development, care and pre-primary education. The report says giving every child at least one year of pre-primary education by 2030 would need more than 35 billion US dollars extra each year (a billion is a thousand million). It says that in the year before primary school more than 90 per cent of children take part in early learning in Europe and Northern America and in Latin America and the Caribbean, but close to 50 per cent in sub-Saharan Africa and in Northern Africa and Western Asia.
g-early-learning.ask: Money for education is limited. Some people think more of it should go to the youngest children, because a good start may help with everything that comes later. Others think primary and secondary schools should come first, because those pupils also need teachers, books and classrooms. If you were in charge of the budget, how would you share it out, and why?
jobs: Pre-primary teacher (a person who helps young children learn before primary school)
Education planner (a person who works out how many schools and teachers a place needs)
Statistician (a person who collects numbers and studies what they show)

g-records-day.ctx: Guinness World Records Day was first held in 2004, and in 2026 it was on Thursday 19 November. David Garibaldi's record was set in New York, the 777 Drifting Team's in Dubai and the three rope-skipping records in Japan. The record for the tightest two-wheel parking is listed as 6.53 metres.
g-records-day.ask: Some records, like car stunts, are risky, while others, like skipping, are things almost anyone can try. Some people think record books should include risky stunts, because skilled performers show what is possible. Others think record books should focus on records that are safer to copy, because young fans may try them. Should record books include risky stunts?
jobs: Stunt driver (a person who performs difficult driving tricks for shows and films)
Record adjudicator (a person who judges whether a record attempt follows the rules)
Performance painter (an artist who paints a picture live in front of an audience)

bigStory.t: How far is one light-day from home?
bigStory.sub: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, reached one light-day from Earth on Wednesday

x.why: A spacecraft that left Earth in 1977 is still travelling. This week it got so far away that light needs a whole day to reach it.

o.why: A spacecraft launched in 1977 is still travelling, and its team on Earth still talks to it. This week it reached a distance so great that a radio signal, moving at the speed of light, needs 24 hours to get there.

facts: about one light-day: how far light travels in 24 hours
how long a radio signal from Earth now takes to reach it
the day it reached one light-day

days.o: NASA launched Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977. It flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, and in 1990 it took a picture of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In 2012 it entered interstellar space, the space between the stars. It is run from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.
days.x: Voyager 1 is a spacecraft. It left Earth in 1977. It flew past the planets Jupiter and Saturn. In 1990 it took a picture of Earth from very far away.

days.o: A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion kilometres. Light reaches the Moon in about 1.3 seconds, and sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. After sunset today, Tuesday 17 November, NASA invites people to flash VGR, Voyager's three-letter call sign, in Morse code towards the sky with a torch.
days.x: A light-day is how far light travels in one day. Sunlight reaches us in about 8 minutes. After sunset today, people can flash a torch for Voyager. Ask a grown-up to help.

days.o: NASA worked out that Voyager 1 would reach one light-day from Earth on Wednesday 18 November. No spacecraft has travelled this far before. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach it, and its reply takes another day to come back. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.
days.x: On Wednesday, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. No spacecraft has gone this far before. A message now takes about a day to get there.

days.o: NASA talks to Voyager 1 by radio through its Deep Space Network, a set of giant radio antennas at three sites: Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. The sites are placed around the world so that they can keep in contact with a spacecraft as Earth turns. Each site has one antenna that is 70 metres across. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and its reply takes another 24 hours to come back, so a message and its answer make a two-day round trip.
days.x: NASA talks to Voyager 1 with radio signals. It uses giant radio antennas in California, Spain and Australia. A message takes about a day to reach Voyager 1. The reply takes another day to come back.

days.o: On Wednesday 18 November Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Its power source makes about 4 watts less every year, so NASA has been switching off instruments to save power. Even after it falls silent, it will keep travelling. It will take about 300 years to reach the inner edge of a distant region called the Oort Cloud. In about 40,000 years it is expected to pass another star. It carries a Golden Record with sounds, music and images from Earth, and greetings in 55 languages.
days.x: On Wednesday, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Its power gets a little weaker every year. Even when it falls silent, it will keep travelling. It carries a Golden Record with sounds, music and pictures from Earth.

poll.q: If you could add one thing to a message carried into space, what would it be?
a: A tune can be enjoyed without knowing the words.
It would show how many peoples share one planet.
A picture can show what words cannot.
A map of where we are
So that whoever finds it knows where it came from.

bigStory.talk: If you sent a message today that would be opened 49 years from now, what would you want the reader to know about your life?

o: A prize for ideas that help the planet
The path an object follows around a planet, moon or star
A senior member of a government
x: From Wednesday, it needs a whole day to reach Voyager 1
A place that keeps and shows interesting and important things
ASEAN's has one more rice stalk
Five winners get one in Mumbai this week

reporters.t: Report one thing that changed in your street or school this week
reporters.why: Monday 16 November was National Press Day in India, and World Children's Day was on Friday 20 November. Good reporters check what they hear with more than one person.
tips: Who told you, and who else can confirm it?
Where and when did it happen?

days.name: World Television Day
days.what: World Television Day is on 21 November. The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the day, which means it announced it officially, on 17 December 1996. It did so because of the growing effect television has on the decisions people make.

days.name: World Fisheries Day
days.what: World Fisheries Day is marked every year on 21 November. It goes back to a meeting of fish workers in New Delhi, India, in 1997. The day draws attention to keeping fishing going in a way that can last, and to the problems it faces.

days.name: World Hello Day
days.what: World Hello Day is on 21 November. It began in 1973. To take part, people say hello to at least 10 people.

born.name: Voltaire
born.what: A writer born in Paris, France. His name at birth was François-Marie Arouet, but he is known as Voltaire. His famous book Candide came out in 1759.

x.t: Why a cyclone gets weaker over land
b: A cyclone is a storm that needs warm sea water.
The warm water feeds the storm. It gives the storm heat and moisture.
When a cyclone moves over land, it loses its warm water. So the storm soon gets weaker.
x.remember: A cyclone gets its power from warm sea water. Over land it loses that warm water and gets weaker.
x.q: What gives a cyclone its power?

o.t: Why a cyclone grows weaker over land
b: Cyclones are storms that need warm ocean water to keep going. Cyclone Akvan grew weaker after it crossed the coast of Odisha on Friday 20 November. Here is why that happens to cyclones.

Warm ocean water is the storm's fuel. It gives the storm heat and moisture. When a cyclone moves over land, that supply is cut off, so the storm weakens quickly. Without the heat and moisture, it is harder for the storm to make the thunderstorms that keep it going.

Some people believe a cyclone weakens over land because of friction, or rubbing, against the ground. Weather agencies say that is not the main reason. The main reason is the loss of heat and moisture from the sea. Cyclones also weaken when they pass over cold water.
o.remember: Warm ocean water is a cyclone's fuel. Over land the storm loses that supply of heat and moisture, so it weakens.
o.q: What is the main reason a cyclone weakens when it moves over land?
a: It loses heat and moisture from the sea

backThen.t: People fly free in a hot-air balloon for the first time
backThen.o: On 21 November 1783, two men became the first people to make a free flight in a hot-air balloon, a flight in a balloon that was not tied to the ground. They were Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and François Laurent, the marquis d'Arlandes. They took off from the grounds of the Château de la Muette in Paris and flew for about 25 minutes. The balloon was made by the brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier. Earlier, on 19 September 1783, the brothers had sent a sheep, a duck and a rooster up in a balloon at Versailles, in front of the royal family. The animals landed safely.
backThen.x: On this day in 1783, two men took off from Paris in a hot-air balloon. The balloon was not tied to the ground. They flew for about 25 minutes.
backThen.why: It was the first time people flew free of the ground.

hiddenWords.o: Record comes from the Latin word recordari, which means to recall or remember. Recordari is built on cor, the Latin word for heart.
Orbit comes from the Latin word orbita, which means a track or rut.
